sources.citation: Merriam, C. Hart. 1930. The New River Indians Tló-hōm-tah'-hoi. American Anthropologist n.s. 32(2): 280-293.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. 35 words from the last speaker Saxy Kidd (pp. 281-282), 12 of them identified as Chimariko, plus a comparison table with Dixon's forms (pp. 285-287). Footnote 1 p. 280: 'All Indian words are written in phonetic English'; primary stress is marked with an apostrophe after the syllable (Ke'-hish, Kap'-ne, Tlo'-hom-tah'-hoi) but no statement about where stress falls.

sources.citation: Kroeber, A. L. 1925. Handbook of the Indians of California. BAE Bulletin 78. Section 'The New River Shasta', pp. 282-283.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing; ethnographic and geographic only. 'Of the three minor Shastan tribes the New River people were perhaps rather nearest to the major group in speech.. In 60 years the tribe melted away without a survivor, leaving only a fragmentary vocabulary' (p. 282).

sources.citation: Dixon, Roland B. 1907. The Shasta. Bulletin of the American Museum of Natural History 17(5): 381-498. Appendix 'The Konomi'hu', pp. 495-498.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on accent. The appendix gives 43 words and 18 phrases (pp. 497-498) recorded in 1903 as 'Konomihu' from a woman recalling her grandfather's speech; Merriam 1930 (pp. 283-287) argues these are in fact New River Shasta (Tlo-hom-tah-hoi). Forms marked with a stress tick (ki'poman, ya'nni, kum'ma, sa'maka..); only comment is 'The whole feeling and sound of the language is, however, very much like the Shasta' (p. 496).

sources.citation: Dixon, Roland B. 1905. The Shasta-Achomawi: A New Linguistic Stock, with Four New Dialects. American Anthropologist n.s. 7(2): 213-217.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. First report of the 'New River dialect' (p. 215: 'much closer to Shasta proper than is the Konomi'hu'); seven New River words in the comparative table pp. 216-217 (gi'ic, kin'nux, ki'oi, ki'tsau, ga'ats, kit'tun, ga'au') carry a stress tick after the stressed syllable but no rule or remark on accent.
